title: Elliott Alphonso Kellis
summary: Elliott Alphonso Kellis (1883–1949) was a Shinnecock boarding-house owner, elected trustee, and community organizer whose public record connects Kellis Rest, land governance, Conscience Point, and a 1938 reservation powwow.
content:
Elliott Alphonso Kellis (1883–1949), also recorded as Elliott A. Kellis, Elliot Kellis, and Elliot Alfonso Kellis, was a Shinnecock boarding-house owner, elected trustee, and organizer whose public record spans more than four decades. His story connects community government, economic life at Kellis Rest, the 1934 land-leasing record, a gathering at Conscience Point, and a 1938 reservation powwow.1

Name and title in the record

The sources vary between Elliott and Elliot and between Alphonso, Alfonso, and the middle initial A. Hunter's printed heading uses “Chief Elliott Alphonso Kellis.” The secure governmental role documented in election records is trustee. This profile preserves “Chief” as a historical title used in the source and does not present it as a separate elected office.2

Kellis Rest

Hunter described Kellis Rest as a boarding house on the Shinnecock Reservation that received overnight guests, summer visitors, and people visiting the church. In 1950 she wrote that the house had formerly belonged to Kellis and was then owned by his widow. The passage records a Shinnecock-owned place of hospitality and business without naming his widow or supplying a marriage date.3

Elected trustee service

Stone's election chronology records Kellis's first trustee election on April 7, 1908 and shows his name recurring in trustee records through 1946. Rather than treating the historical title “Chief” as the office, these records document his repeated elected service within the trustee system that governed reservation affairs during this period.4

Land, gathering, and public cultural work

Hunter associated Elliott A. Kellis with a 1934 initiative concerning leases of unused reservation land. Her account is a historical snapshot of governance and land policy in that period, not a description of present Shinnecock government. A separate circa-1934 photograph at Conscience Point names Elliot Kellis among a group of Shinnecock participants; the caption documents his presence but does not assign him a specific performance or role.5

In 1938, records associate Elliot Kellis and artist Zella de Milhau with organizing a powwow on the Shinnecock Reservation. The event belongs to the longer public history of gatherings at Shinnecock, but this profile does not describe it as the beginning of the living Shinnecock Powwow tradition.6

Reading the map

The map chronology connects broad or public places in Kellis's documented record: the Shinnecock Reservation, Conscience Point, and the Shinnecock Powwow Grounds. The line orders records by date; it is not a reconstruction of his exact travel route or private residence.

References

  • Shinnecock Indian Nation Ancestors from 19th and 20th Century, Elliott A. Kellis entry.
  • Lois Marie Hunter, The Shinnecock Indians (Buys Bros., 1950), scanned PDF pp. 7 and 31–32 / printed pp. 12–13 and 60–63.
  • Gaynell Stone, ed., The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History, vol. VI (1983), p. 115 and trustee-election chronology, pp. 345 and 351.
  • David Bunn Martine, Shinnecock History Timeline, p. 11.
why_this_matters: Elliott Alphonso Kellis’s record shows how Shinnecock public life joined economic initiative, hospitality, elected service, land governance, and community gatherings. Reading those activities together makes a long history of practical self-government visible without turning a historical title or one event into a larger claim than the sources support.
activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported biography of Elliott Alphonso Kellis with Kellis Rest, elected trustee service, three linked Historic Moments, and a public-location chronology that distinguishes his historical title from an elected office.
